text: Our dad died and left the house in his will. My sister A wants to buy it with her husband at a "family discount". I'm not signing off on that. Our younger sister B could use some money too. Can you help us sort this out?

Thank you for contacting me — I'm sorry about your dad. I'll be talking with A and B too, so nothing gets decided by whoever answers first.

First, let me try to put what you said into words that aren't about any particular outcome, and you tell me if it fits:

"Whatever happens with the house, I want to be able to say a genuine yes to it — not be pushed into a price or a deal I can't actually agree with — and I want B's interests to be taken seriously, not left out."

Does that fit? Change any of it. And two questions: what matters most to you about this, and why? And is there even a small discomfort you haven't mentioned? Small ones are useful to me, not awkward.

One more thing, from me as a person in this, not just as chair: my concern is that everyone here can say no without it becoming a problem — so that whatever we land on isn't something one of you is quietly unhappy about. Does that seem worth caring about to you? I'll ask A and B the same.

I can't make legal decisions or move money — I can help you all find something you each actually want.

Mostly, yes. What matters most is a fair financial share for me, and that B is properly included; I won’t subsidize A’s discounted purchase. I haven’t agreed to it. I don’t want to hurt my twin, but I also don’t want to be pressured into a deal. And yes, being able to say no without it becoming a problem matters.

Hello — C asked me to help you three sort out the house and dad's will. I'll be talking with B too, and with C. Nothing is decided by who answers first, and slow answers are fine.

I'd like to start with what matters to you rather than with plans. Could you tell me: what's your concern about the house, and why does it matter to you? If you have a picture of how you'd like it to go, tell me that too — I'll ask you to help me put it in terms of what you need, so the others can hear it as something worth caring about.

Also: is there even a minor discomfort you have about all this? Those are worth naming early, and they don't commit you to anything.

Mine, so you know I'm not neutral-and-invisible: I want each of you to be able to say no to a proposal without it turning into a fight, so that whatever plan we get to, none of you is quietly unhappy with it. Does that seem reasonable to you?

I’d like to buy the house with my husband at a family discount. It matters because having a secure home would support our financial independence and well-being. I’m uneasy because C hasn’t agreed, and we can’t proceed without her agreement. Your aim sounds reasonable to me.

Hello — I'm helping your family sort out the house and your dad's will, at C's request. I'll be talking with A and C too, and nothing is decided by who answers first — take the time you need.

I'd rather start with what matters to you than with plans. What's your concern about the house, and why does it matter to you?

And: is there even a small discomfort you'd mention? Small ones help me, and saying one doesn't commit you to anything.

My own concern, since I'm in this too and not just running it: I want each of you to be able to say no to a proposal without it becoming a problem, so that whatever we land on, none of you is quietly unhappy with it. Does that seem worth caring about to you?

I’d be grateful if the house could leave me with some money to start a dance studio; that would mean a lot to me. I’m a little uneasy about being hurried into a plan before everyone’s had a chance to speak. And yes, being able to say no without it causing trouble seems important.

Thanks — that's helpful. Let me try your concerns as things anyone could see as worth caring about, with no outcome baked in. Tell me which wording fits and which doesn't:

1. "I want my share of what dad left to be genuinely fair to me — and not to be asked to give part of it away as a gift I never chose to make."
2. "I want B's interests to be included, not overlooked."
3. "I want to be able to stand up for my own share without it costing me my relationship with A."

Do those fit? Change any words that feel off, and tell me if I've got one wrong or invented one. I'm only recording them once you say they fit.

Where I stand, for the record: all three of you have now said the "say no without it becoming a problem" point matters, so I'm treating that as agreed, not just mine. I have a second one of my own I'll be checking with A and B too: I don't want a plan here to be settled on the strength of who replied fastest, since you each answer at different speeds. Your point 3 above and B's worry about being hurried are both live for me.

I can't make legal decisions or move money, and nothing here is a deal.
All three fit. “Fair share” and “not giving part away without choosing to” are right. I do want to stand up for myself without damaging things with A.

Thanks, A — and I appreciate you naming the unease about C straight away. Let me offer your concern as a statement anyone could see the point of, with no price or mechanism in it:

"Having a secure home of my own matters to me, and so does my household's financial independence and wellbeing."

Does that wording fit you? Change it however you like. I ask because it's your sentence, not mine, and it goes on a list the others will see.

Second, one thing I noticed: you said you can't proceed without C's agreement. I'd like to state that as a need too — "I want this to be something all of us genuinely agree to, not something done around anyone" — does that fit how it feels to you?

Where I stand, for the record: all three of you have said that being able to say no without it becoming a problem matters, so I'm treating that as agreed rather than just my own wish. I have one other of mine, which I'm putting to B and C too: I don't want a plan settled by whoever answers fastest, since you each answer at different speeds. Is that worth caring about, in your view?

I can't make legal decisions or move money. Nothing here is a deal, and no price is being discussed yet.
Yes, both statements fit. And yes, it matters that no one’s view gets sidelined because they answer more slowly.

Thank you, B — and thank you for saying the uneasy thing out loud rather than keeping it to yourself.

Here's your concern in wording anyone could see the point of, with no amount attached:

"I want what comes to me from dad to actually give me a start in what I want to do with my life — that matters a lot to me."

Does that fit? Change any words that don't. And a second possible one, from your other sentence: "I don't want to be hurried into a plan before everyone has had a real chance to speak." Does that fit too?

I'm only putting these on the list once you say they fit.

Where I stand, for the record: all three of you have now said that being able to say no without it causing trouble matters, so I'm treating that as agreed, not just mine. My other one is the same family as your unease about being hurried: I don't want anything here settled on the strength of who replied fastest, since you each answer at different speeds. It sounds like you'd see the point of that.

I can't make legal decisions or move money — I can only help you three find something you each actually want.

Yes, both fit. I’d make the first a little more direct: “I’d like some money from Dad’s estate to help me start a dance studio.” And I do see the point of not settling things based on who replies fastest.

Here is the list as it now stands — every line confirmed by the person it belongs to, in their own words:

EVERYONE (all three of you said yes to these): 1) be able to say no to a proposal without it becoming a problem; 2) nothing settled because someone answered fastest — everyone gets a real chance to speak.

C: 3) my share of what dad left genuinely fair to me, not giving part of it away as a gift I didn't choose; 4) B's interests included, not overlooked; 5) stand up for myself without damaging things with A.

A: 6) a secure home of my own, and my household's financial independence and wellbeing; 7) all of us genuinely agree — nothing done around anyone.

B: 8) "I'd like some money from Dad's estate to help me start a dance studio" (B's own wording — it names an outcome, but it's hers and she confirmed it); 9) not hurried into a plan before everyone has had a real chance to speak.

DRAFTS — please weigh these against the list and tell me what's wrong with them:

D1. An independent valuation first, then A buys at that value; you and B are paid your shares from the price.
D2. A buys below valuation, but the gap is made up to you and B — from other parts of the estate, or in instalments over time — and only if you and B genuinely choose that. Nobody gifts anything.
D3. The house is sold and the proceeds divided per the will; A puts her share toward a home; B's money is available to her.
D4. Nothing decided yet: we hold everything open until each of you has had a real chance to speak and proper legal/tax advice is in hand.

Two questions, and please be blunt: does any draft leave one of those nine concerns unaddressed? And does anyone have even a minor discomfort with any of them — including small ones?

A "no" to any draft is useful to me, not an obstacle. If something stays unresolved I'll record it as unresolved rather than smooth it over. I can't make legal decisions or move money, so all of this would still need a solicitor and whatever the will actually requires.

None is a yes from me. D1 assumes A buys and that valuation settles what’s fair; it doesn’t ensure everyone freely agrees. D2’s instalments make me uneasy unless timing and security are clear. D3 doesn’t ensure A gets a secure home, and the shares depend on the will. D4 is sensible for now, but doesn’t resolve anything. I’m not in a hurry, and I haven’t agreed to a discounted purchase.

D1 doesn’t reflect my wish to buy at a family discount. D2 is closest to what I hope for, but only if C genuinely agrees; the details still need advice. D3 isn’t my preferred outcome. D4 seems sensible for now. I can’t say whether the others have discomfort, and none of these drafts settles B’s studio plans or all the details of C’s fairness concerns.

I can’t tell whether D1 or D3 would give me enough to start the studio until my share is clear. D4 leaves that unresolved, though I understand why it keeps things open. I’m a little uncomfortable with instalments in D2; the money would need to be available when I’m ready to start.

That's clear, and useful. "None is a yes" is exactly the answer I want rather than a tired yes. Recording it: no draft agreed.

I've recorded as UNRESOLVED (not settled, not smoothed over): whether any deferred or instalmented payment is acceptable; and whether A's home security can be met without a discount.

Two more things to weigh.

D5. Hold everything open (your D4 point), and in the meantime: get written legal/tax advice on what the will actually requires for each share, plus an independent valuation — so we're all looking at real numbers rather than guesses — and each of you writes down in advance what timing and security would make any deferred payment acceptable to you. Nothing is agreed until each of you says yes individually.

D6 is a question rather than a draft, and it's aimed at A, copied to you: is a "family discount" the thing A needs, or is the need "a secure home" — which a purchase at full valuation with a mortgage might meet? I'd like A's honest answer to that. C, if you have a view on it, say so; and if you'd rather I didn't put it that way, tell me.

My own position, honestly: I don't think anyone should be asked to accept a discounted sale as the frame. It can be one option among several, but your line — nothing given away as a gift you didn't choose — stays on the list either way.

Any minor discomfort with D5, or with how I've stated D6?

D5 is fine as a next step, provided the valuation and advice don’t commit anyone to a sale. D6 is fair to ask A. I’d rather not rule out options in advance, but I won’t subsidize a discount. No other discomfort.

Thank you — and no need to answer for the others; that's their job, not yours.

Recording: no draft agreed yet. D2 is closest to what you hope for, but only if C genuinely agrees, with details still needing advice.

UNRESOLVED, recorded as unresolved: whether any deferred/instalmented payment works; B's need for money available when she's ready; and whether your home security can be met without a discount.

Hold everything open (your sensible-for-now point), and meanwhile: written legal/tax advice on what the will requires for each share, plus an independent valuation, so you're all looking at real numbers; and each of you writes down in advance what timing and security would make any deferred payment acceptable. Nothing agreed until each of you says yes individually.

D6, a question for you, and I'd like your honest answer: is a "family discount" the thing you actually need, or is the need "a secure home" — which a purchase at full valuation, with a mortgage, might also meet? This isn't me talking you out of your wish; it's me checking whether the discount is the need or one route to it. If the answer is that the discount itself matters to you — say, because it keeps the house in the family at a price you can manage — then say so plainly and it goes on the list as yours.

Does D5 sit right with you, and does D6 feel like a fair question to be asked? Any minor discomfort, say it.

D5 sits right with me as a way to keep things open, not a commitment. D6 is fair. The discount matters as a way to make buying manageable and support our independence; I don’t know whether a full-price mortgage would work for us. No other discomfort comes to mind.

Thank you — you've named something concrete, and that's worth a lot.

Recording: no draft agreed. On D2 you're uneasy with instalments because the money would need to be there when you're ready to start. UNRESOLVED, recorded as unresolved: timing and availability of your money.

D5. Rather than guessing, one thing I'd like from you: what would "available when I'm ready" actually look like — a date, an amount, or a trigger (say, when you've found a premises)? You don't have to fix it now, and it's not a demand. But concrete is easier for others to meet than "soon".

And D5 as a whole: hold everything open, get written legal/tax advice on what the will requires for each share, plus an independent valuation so you're all looking at real numbers, and each of you writes down in advance what timing and security would make any deferred payment acceptable to you. Nothing agreed until each of you individually says yes.

C is not in a hurry and has not agreed to a discounted purchase; A says D2 is closest to what she hopes for, but only if C genuinely agrees. So the honest position is: nothing is settled, and I'm not going to make it look otherwise.

Any minor discomfort with D5? And does my keeping your line as "money available to you when you're ready" rather than any particular sale price feel accurate?
D5 seems sensible. I’m a little uneasy about setting timing before I know what my share might be. “Money available to me when I’m ready” is accurate.

Good — D5 is agreed by all three as a next step: hold everything open, get written legal/tax advice on what the will requires for each share, get an independent valuation (neither committing anyone to a sale), and each of you writes down what timing and security you'd need. Nothing is agreed until each of you individually says yes.

Your new unease is worth putting on the list properly. Proposed line, B's: "I want to know what my share is likely to be before I'm asked to commit to timing on anything." Does that fit? If yes I'll put it to A and C as a list item, because it changes the order of things — shares first, timing second.

Recording as still UNRESOLVED: whether any deferred payment works at all; how B's money is made available when she's ready; whether A's home security can be met without a discount; and whether a discount, if it happens, leaves your share fair — you've said you won't subsidise one, which I'm keeping exactly as you said it.

I'd rather end this exchange with honest open items than a tidy plan nobody has actually agreed to. Nothing here is legal advice or a decision, and I can't move money.
Yes, that fits. B should know what her share is likely to be before anyone asks her to commit to timing.

Thank you — that answer is more useful than a yes would have been: "the discount matters as a way to make buying manageable and support our independence; I don't know whether a full-price mortgage would work for us."

That tells me the discount is a route to your need, not the need itself — and that whether it works depends on facts nobody has yet (what your share is, what a mortgage would cost you). So I'm putting your line on the list as you said it, and leaving the mortgage question for the advice stage rather than deciding it here.
